title: Self-improvement with search and deep research agents
big_idea: You can make an agent better without training it by searching. Search over answers: draw many programs, keep the ones that pass the examples, group them by behavior, and submit one per group. Search for knowledge: let the model pause mid-thought, look something up, boil the results down, and keep reasoning.

papers.title: Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode
papers.what: A transformer model sampled up to millions of programs per competitive-programming problem. It filtered them with the example tests from the problem statement, then clustered the survivors by their outputs on new test inputs written by a separate model, and submitted one program per cluster, largest first, with at most 10 submissions.
papers.result: Average ranking in the top 54.3% in simulated Codeforces contests with more than 5,000 participants. Solved 34.2% of held-out CodeContests problems with up to a million samples and 10 submissions. Filtering on example tests removed about 99% of samples. Solve rate grew roughly log-linearly with the number of samples.
papers.takeaway: When a cheap exact check exists (example tests), sample a lot and filter. When many candidates survive, group them by behavior and pick from the biggest group, because correct programs tend to agree with each other.

papers.title: AlphaCode 2 Technical Report
papers.authors: AlphaCode Team, Google DeepMind (Leblond et al.)
papers.what: The same sample, filter and cluster pipeline, built on fine-tuned Gemini Pro models. It drew up to a million C++ samples per problem with randomized temperature, kept the 10 largest clusters, and added a second fine-tuned Gemini model that scores each sample's chance of being correct to choose the best one in each cluster.
papers.result: Solved 43% of problems from 12 recent Codeforces contests (77 problems) within 10 attempts, vs 25% for the original AlphaCode. Estimated 85th percentile among participants (AlphaCode: about 46%). Filtering removed about 95% of samples. Needed about 100 samples to match AlphaCode with a million samples.
papers.takeaway: A better base model makes search far more sample-efficient, and a learned scorer helps choose inside a group. Selection, not generation, is often where the remaining gains are.

papers.title: Search-o1: Agentic Search-Enhanced Large Reasoning Models
papers.what: A reasoning model (QwQ-32B-Preview) writes a search query between special tags whenever it is unsure. The system pauses, retrieves the top 10 web results, and a separate Reason-in-Documents step condenses them into the facts that matter, which are inserted back into the reasoning chain.
papers.result: On GPQA diamond, overall 63.6 vs 58.1 for the same model without retrieval and 58.6 with standard RAG. Averaged over the five reasoning datasets it beat agentic RAG without Reason-in-Documents by 4.7% and no retrieval by 3.1%. On multi-hop QA, average exact match beat standard RAG by 29.6% and agentic RAG by 5.3%.
papers.takeaway: For multi-step questions, let the model decide when and what to search, one fact at a time, and condense the results before they reach the reasoning. One retrieval with the whole question often misses the second hop.

terms: Throwing away candidate programs that fail the example tests given in the problem.
Running candidates on extra inputs and grouping the ones that give identical outputs; the inputs need no known answers.
Percent of problems solved when k samples are drawn but only 10 may be submitted.
A model that predicts how likely a code sample is to be correct, used to rank samples.
Retrieval where the model itself decides when to search and what to search for, possibly many times.
A separate step that reads retrieved pages and writes back only the useful facts, so noisy text does not derail reasoning.
Fraction of problems where at least one sample is correct; the ceiling for any selection method.
traps: Passing the example tests is not being correct. Many wrong programs pass them, which is why AlphaCode needed clustering and hidden tests.
Random selection wastes your submission budget on programs that are written differently but behave the same.
Clustering inputs only need to separate programs. They do not need known answers, and even invalid inputs can help.
Naive RAG retrieves once with the whole question. For two-hop questions it often gets one hop and misses the other.
Pasting long raw search results into a reasoning chain can push it off track. Condense first.
A small model may never emit a search, or may search with vague words. Read the transcripts, not just the score.
check: Why does AlphaCode pick from the largest cluster first?
There are many ways to be wrong but correct programs tend to behave the same, so they gather in larger clusters.
What did AlphaCode 2 add on top of filtering and clustering?
A fine-tuned Gemini scoring model that picks the best sample in each of the 10 largest clusters.
About how much did filtering with example tests remove in AlphaCode?
It reads the retrieved documents with the current reasoning and query, and returns only the relevant facts to insert into the reasoning chain.
In our notebook, why can naive RAG fail on the approver question?
The question needs the contract's monthly fee and the procurement policy tiers; one retrieval with the whole question may bring back only one of them.
